eras.name: Classic learners
eras.background: Statistical learning theory explained when models generalize, and practical learners followed: decision trees, maximum-margin classifiers and ensembles. Averaging or boosting many trees proved the most reliable way to handle tabular data.

eras.name: Boosting at scale
eras.text: Fast boosted trees win tabular data
eras.background: As datasets grew, engineering made gradient-boosted trees fast on large, sparse data. They dominated competitions and production tabular models, and tools to explain them followed.

eras.name: Pretrained models
eras.background: Deep learning had long lagged boosted trees on tables. Pretraining a Transformer on synthetic datasets finally produced a model that predicts small tables in context, without training on them.

nodes.label: CART
nodes.problem: Classification rules were written by experts.
nodes.idea: Grow a tree that splits the data on one feature at a time.
nodes.impact: Readable models, and the building block of forests and boosting.

nodes.label: SVM
nodes.problem: Models that fit the training data well often generalized poorly.
nodes.idea: Find the widest-margin boundary, with kernels for nonlinear shapes.
nodes.impact: Led many benchmarks until deep learning and boosted trees took over.

nodes.label: AdaBoost
nodes.problem: Simple models alone are only weak learners.
nodes.idea: Train learners in sequence, reweighting the examples earlier ones got wrong.
nodes.impact: Showed weak learners add up to a strong one, the basis of boosting.

nodes.label: Random forests
nodes.idea: Average many trees, each grown on a random sample with random features.
nodes.impact: Accurate with little tuning, and a default baseline for tabular data.

from.why: Single trees overfit and change a lot with small changes in the data.

nodes.label: Gradient boosting
nodes.idea: Friedman fits each new tree to the gradient of any differentiable loss.
nodes.impact: Gradient-boosted trees became the strongest method on tabular data.

from.why: AdaBoost was tied to one loss function.
Supplied the regression trees that each boosting step fits.

nodes.label: XGBoost
nodes.idea: Sparsity-aware splits, quantile sketches and cache-aware computation.
nodes.impact: Won most tabular competitions and spread through industry.

from.why: Gradient boosting was slow on large, sparse datasets.

nodes.label: LightGBM
nodes.idea: Sample rows by gradient and bundle sparse features that never overlap.
nodes.impact: Much faster training on large data, alongside XGBoost and CatBoost.

from.why: Finding splits still scanned every row and every feature.

nodes.label: TreeSHAP
nodes.idea: Compute exact Shapley values for trees in polynomial time.
nodes.impact: SHAP plots became the usual way to explain tree models.

from.why: Tree ensembles were accurate but hard to explain.
Boosted models were now everywhere, and each prediction needed an explanation.

nodes.label: TabPFN
nodes.idea: Pretrain a Transformer on synthetic datasets so it predicts new tables in context.
nodes.impact: Beats tuned boosted trees on small tables without training on them.

from.why: Boosted trees must be trained and tuned again for every new table.

main.title: UC Berkeley CS 188: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
main.why: Search, games, MDPs and reinforcement learning, Bayes nets and HMMs, then decision trees, naive Bayes and neural networks, with Pacman projects. In English.

main.title: Stanford CS229: Machine Learning
main.why: Linear models and GLMs, generative models, kernels, neural networks, bias-variance and regularization, then k-means, EM, factor analysis, PCA and ICA. In English.

main.title: Cornell CS4780: Machine Learning for Intelligent Systems
main.why: Decision and regression trees, bagging, random forests and boosting. In English.

main.title: Support-Vector Networks
main.why: For good generalization, SVM fits the widest-margin boundary in a high-dimensional feature space, with a soft margin that allows some errors.

main.title: Random Forests
main.why: Single decision trees overfit, so random forests average many trees, each grown on a random sample with random features.

main.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
main.why: Gradient boosting was slow on large, sparse data, so XGBoost adds sparsity-aware splits, a weighted quantile sketch and cache-aware, out-of-core computation.

main.title: LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree
main.why: GBDT scans every row and feature to find splits, so LightGBM samples rows by gradient and bundles mutually exclusive features.

main.title: CatBoost: Unbiased Boosting with Categorical Features
main.why: Target statistics for categorical features leak the label into training, so CatBoost uses ordered boosting to remove the bias.

main.title: Explainable AI for Trees: From Local Explanations to Global Understanding
main.why: Exact Shapley values take exponential time, but TreeSHAP computes them for tree models in polynomial time.

main.title: Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model
main.why: Boosted trees must be trained and tuned for each table, so TabPFN pretrains a Transformer on synthetic datasets to predict new small tables in context.
Ad click prediction needs calibrated probabilities at scale, so Facebook feeds boosted-tree features into a logistic regression and retrains often.

main.title: Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance
main.why: Models can look accurate because training data leaks the answer, and this paper defines leakage and how to detect and avoid it.

main.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
main.why: In production ML the model is a small part, while glue code, data dependencies and feedback loops pile up maintenance debt.
